newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian official warns about riots over power cuts.
newsitem.headline: Indian official warns about riots over power cuts.

text.p: Indians used to religious riots may see energy riots as the nation's power shortage was assuming alarming proportions, a top civil servant warned on Thursday.
"You may see riots -- not in the communal sense, but for lack of power," P.Abraham, secretary of the federal ministry of power told reporters after addressing a business conference.
"There will be no water in your taps, hospitals will be closed...," Abraham warned. People in the Indian capital New Delhi were without power on New Year's day, he said.
Abraham said he was not exaggerating but warning the public in his capacity as the senior-most bureaucrat of his ministry.
Power had become as fundamental a requirement as food, clothing and shelter, he said.
Referring to the blackout in the capital on New Year's day, Abraham said the power secretary's role was reduced to that of a "grid operator" monitoring each power station.
Consumers in cities like Delhi and Bombay were lucky because they were supplied with power even if it meant starving interior towns and villages, the secretary said.
In the northern Haryana state bordering Delhi, there was no power for five days a week. Rajasthan state, also bordering the capital, went without power for three days a week.
Electricity is available in southernmost Kerala state for only just one third of each day due to power cuts.
He said the situation was liable to worsen in the summer months. People switch on air conditioners and fans to cope with the heat
Only 60 percent of the power supplied in Delhi was billed and collections amounted to only 40 percent of the billing, he said.
In Bombay people paid up because distribution was in private hands, Abraham said, pleading for more privatisation.
Power supplied to farmers was subsidised by 100 billion ($2.8 billion) rupees a year about half which was paid by Indian states and the rest was written off.
Many states were charging consumers at rates lower than the cost of supply as the tariff was too politically sensitive.
India had a 10 percent energy shortage (20 percent peak hour shortage) equivalent to about 10,000 MW a year, Abraham said.

He said the government would soon introduce laws to amend the electricity act and set up independent regulatory commissions to fix tariffs to ensure a minimum of three percent return to utility companies.
Foreign firms wanting to build power plants will be given automatic approval provided their ownership of the Indian projects do not exceed 74 percent, Abraham said.
The provinces will be given authority to approve thermal power stations upto 250 MW.
Abraham visualised the focus shifting from approvals to financing. Over 40 projects are now pending with financial institutions and 21 have received clearance in principle.
Power projects alone required 3,000 billion rupees over the next five years, Abraham said.
